title: Cancellation and timeouts
goal: By the end you can make CPU loops and blocking calls respond to cancellation, keep CancellationException flowing instead of swallowing it, run suspending cleanup after a cancel, and choose between withTimeout and withTimeoutOrNull.

warmup.q: A coroutine on `Dispatchers.Default` runs `for (t in transactions) score(t)` over two million transactions, with no suspend calls inside the loop. Another coroutine calls `job.cancel()` halfway through. What happens?
options: The loop stops at once, because `cancel()` stops the coroutine's thread
The loop stops at the next iteration, because the compiler adds a check to every loop
The loop runs to the end, and only then does the job finish as cancelled
`cancel()` throws `IllegalStateException`, because the coroutine is busy
warmup.why: Cancellation is cooperative. `cancel()` only marks the job as cancelling. The coroutine notices at its next suspension point or explicit check, and this loop has neither, so it finishes all two million transactions first. Java's `Future.cancel(true)` has the same limit: it sets a flag that someone has to read.

sections.h: Timeouts are cancellation with a clock

steps: Read `TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt`. The issuer takes 1.5 s and every call gets 300 ms. Predict the outcome and the time for each line.
Run it.

code.title: TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt

alt.title: TimeoutsAndBlockingJava.java

try.expect: The two `delay` cases end at about 300 ms: one throws, one returns null. The `withContext(IO)` case throws too, but only after about 1,500 ms, when the sleep is over. `runInterruptible` returns null at about 300 ms. After your change, the bare sleep returns `approved` after 1,500 ms: the block never suspended, so the timeout was ignored. In the Java twin, `orTimeout` gives the caller its exception on time while the abandoned call finishes at 1,500 ms anyway; `cancel(true)` interrupts it at about 300 ms.

analogy: Cancelling a coroutine is like a manager putting a "stop, we're closing" note on each worker's desk. A worker who looks up between tasks (a suspension point) sees it, tidies up and goes home. A worker deep in a long calculation who never looks up keeps going until the calculation is done. A worker on hold with a supplier (a blocking call) can't see the desk at all until someone taps them on the shoulder, which is what `runInterruptible` does. `runCatching` is the worker who reads the note, throws it in the bin and starts the next task. `NonCancellable` is the exemption for tidying up: "finish putting the cash in the safe, then go." The analogy breaks in one place: binning the note doesn't make it go away. Every desk the worker sits at afterwards has the same note on it.
in_your_world: Cancellation reaches your payment code more often than you think. A Kafka rebalance revokes a partition, and its worker's scope is cancelled. A Quarkus shutdown cancels long-lived scopes in `@PreDestroy`. Every `withTimeout` on an issuer call is a cancel waiting to happen. Three things keep that safe. Never wrap a suspend call in `runCatching` or `catch (e: Exception)` without rethrowing `CancellationException`, or a shutdown turns into a list of fake failures. Release card holds, distributed locks and idempotency claims in `finally` with `withContext(NonCancellable)`. And remember that an Oracle query running in `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` ignores the timeout around it: use `runInterruptible` only if the driver responds to interrupts, and set `Statement.setQueryTimeout` either way. Temporal works on the same idea: an activity learns that it has been cancelled only when it heartbeats.
mistake: The most common mistake is swallowing `CancellationException` with a catch-all: `runCatching { }`, `catch (e: Exception)` or `catch (e: Throwable)` around a suspend call, usually written to "log and keep going" in a batch or polling loop. It looks like good defensive code, and it works perfectly until the first shutdown or timeout. Then the loop either reports every remaining item as failed or spins at full CPU, and a cancelled job seems to hang or to finish with nonsense. The fix: rethrow `CancellationException` before handling anything else (`if (e is CancellationException) throw e`), or catch only the exception types you expect from the call.

compare.title: Stopping a CPU loop: Future.cancel(true) vs Job.cancel()

java.title: ReconciliationJob.java

kotlin.title: ReconciliationJob.kt

compare.note: Both models are cooperative, and both loops need the same explicit check. The differences are in what carries the request. Java's interrupt is a flag on a thread. Catching `InterruptedException` clears it, so a swallowed interrupt is lost, and the request doesn't reach other threads the task started. A coroutine's cancellation is a state on its job. It stays set, it flows down to every child in the tree, and every suspension point checks it. The two also see different things: blocking JDK calls react to interrupts but not to job cancellation (bridge them with `runInterruptible`), while suspension points react to job cancellation and ignore the interrupt flag.

worked.title: Make a chargeback poller stop cleanly

steps.say: A poller checks a chargeback's status every 5 s until the card scheme decides. It holds a lease (a row lock in Oracle) so only one pod polls each case. During a deploy, pods take 30 s to shut down, and leases stay locked until they expire. Find the three problems before reading on.
Problem 1: `catch (e: Exception)` swallows the `CancellationException` from `delay`, so a cancelled poller spins. Catch only the scheme client's error, and let cancellation through.

Problem 2: the lease release suspends in a cancelled coroutine, so it throws before it reaches Oracle. Wrap it in `NonCancellable`, with its own short timeout so a stuck database can't hold up shutdown.
Problem 3: nothing bounds the whole poll. Give the caller a deadline, and treat running out as an expected outcome rather than an exception.

Self-check: the timeout in step 3 cancels `pollChargeback` while it is suspended in `delay`. Trace what happens. (The `delay` throws `TimeoutCancellationException`, it passes the narrow `catch`, the `finally` releases the lease under `NonCancellable`, and `withTimeoutOrNull` turns the exception into `null`.)

recap: Cancellation is cooperative. `cancel()` marks the job, and the coroutine stops at its next suspension point or explicit check. CPU loops need `ensureActive()`, `isActive` or `yield()`.
Cancellation travels as `CancellationException`. `runCatching`, `catch (e: Exception)` and `catch (e: Throwable)` all catch it, so rethrow it or catch narrower types.
In a cancelled coroutine every suspension point throws at once. Run suspending cleanup in `finally` inside `withContext(NonCancellable)`, and never pass `NonCancellable` to `launch` or `async`.

`withTimeout` throws `TimeoutCancellationException` (a `CancellationException`), and `withTimeoutOrNull` returns `null`. Inside `launch`, a timeout doesn't fail the parent unless you turn it into an error.
Timeouts can't stop blocking calls. Wrap interruptible blocking code in `runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO)`, and give clients such as JDBC their own timeouts.
`flow { }` checks for cancellation on each `emit`; `asFlow()` doesn't, so add `.cancellable()`.

quiz.q: `val job = scope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) { while (true) { digest.update(nextBlock()) } }`, where `nextBlock()` is a plain function. You call `job.cancelAndJoin()`. What happens?
options: It returns at once, because `cancel` stops the coroutine
It returns after the current loop iteration
It never returns: the loop has no suspension point and never checks
The caller gets a `CancellationException` thrown from `cancelAndJoin`
quiz.why: Nothing in the loop looks at the job, so the cancel request is never noticed, and `cancelAndJoin` waits forever. Add `ensureActive()` or `yield()` to the loop, or loop on `while (isActive)`.

quiz.q: A coroutine was cancelled while it waited in `delay`. Its `finally` block must call the suspending `lease.release()`. Which line does that correctly?
options: `try { lease.release() } catch (e: CancellationException) { }`
`withContext(NonCancellable) { lease.release() }`
`launch(NonCancellable) { lease.release() }`
`GlobalScope.launch { lease.release() }`
quiz.why: Inside `withContext(NonCancellable)` suspension points don't throw, so the release runs to the end, and the cancel carries on afterwards. Catching the exception just loses the release. `launch(NonCancellable)` and `GlobalScope` both start a coroutine outside the tree that nothing waits for, so shutdown can finish before the release does.

options: `done`, after about 100 ms
Nothing: `coroutineScope` throws `TimeoutCancellationException`
`done`, after about 1,000 ms
Nothing: the program hangs
quiz.why: `TimeoutCancellationException` is a `CancellationException`, so the child counts as cancelled, not failed, and the scope completes normally. If a timeout must fail the caller, write `withTimeoutOrNull(100) { ... } ?: error("timed out")`.

quiz.q: `withTimeout(500) { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { Thread.sleep(3_000) } }`. How long does the caller wait, and what does it get?
options: About 500 ms, then `TimeoutCancellationException`
About 500 ms, then `null`
About 3 s, then `TimeoutCancellationException`
About 3 s, then the block's result
quiz.why: The timer fires at 500 ms and cancels the coroutine, but `Thread.sleep` doesn't see it. When the sleep ends, `withContext` checks, finds the job cancelled, and the timeout surfaces as the exception. `runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO)` would interrupt the sleep at 500 ms.

quiz.q: From the executors track: a task is blocked in `Thread.sleep(5_000)` when someone calls `future.cancel(true)` on it. What happens to the task?
options: Nothing until the sleep ends, then it carries on
The thread is stopped and the task's `finally` blocks are skipped
The future completes normally with `null`
`sleep` throws `InterruptedException` at once, and the task can clean up and stop
quiz.why: `cancel(true)` interrupts the worker thread, and `sleep` responds to interrupts by throwing. What the task does next is up to its code: restore the flag and stop, or swallow it and carry on. That is the Java version of `runInterruptible`.

flashcards.front: Does `job.cancel()` stop a CPU loop with no suspend calls?
flashcards.back: No. Cancellation is cooperative: the loop must call `ensureActive()` or `yield()`, or check `isActive`.

flashcards.front: What does a suspension point such as `delay` do in a cancelled coroutine?
flashcards.back: It throws `CancellationException` at once, without suspending.

flashcards.front: Why is `runCatching { suspendCall() }` risky inside a coroutine?
flashcards.back: It catches every `Throwable`, `CancellationException` included, so the coroutine carries on after it was cancelled. Rethrow `CancellationException`.

flashcards.front: How do you call a suspending cleanup function in `finally` after a cancel?
On timeout, what do `withTimeout` and `withTimeoutOrNull` do?

flashcards.back: No. Blocking calls ignore cancellation. Wrap them in `runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { ... }` so the thread is interrupted.

flashcards.front: `(1..1_000).asFlow().collect { ... }`: does each element check for cancellation?
flashcards.back: No. `asFlow()` doesn't check. Add `.cancellable()`. A `flow { }` builder checks on every `emit`.

terms.plain: Cancelling only asks; the code stops when it next checks or reaches a suspension point.
A call to a suspend function such as `delay`, `await` or `withContext`. Library ones check for cancellation.
The exception that carries a cancel through the coroutine's code. Catching it without rethrowing breaks cancellation.
A job that is always active. `withContext(NonCancellable)` lets cleanup suspend after a cancel.
What `withTimeout` throws. It is a `CancellationException`, so a parent treats it as a cancel, not a failure.
Runs blocking code on a dispatcher and interrupts its thread if the coroutine is cancelled.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate wrapped every call in a settlement loop in `runCatching` "so one bad batch never stops the run". After the last deploy, the shutdown logs listed forty failed batches that had never failed. Explain what happened and how you'd change the code.
explain_back.answer: When the pod shut down, the settlement coroutine was cancelled. Cancellation reaches the code as a CancellationException thrown from the next suspension point, and runCatching catches every Throwable, so it caught that too and logged the batch in progress as failed. The coroutine was still cancelled, so the next batch threw at its first suspension point, got caught and logged the same way, and so on through all forty remaining batches. Then the function returned normally. I'd keep the per-batch error handling but rethrow CancellationException before logging anything, or catch only the exceptions the settle call is expected to throw. Then a cancel ends the run at the batch in progress, and any cleanup that suspends goes in a finally inside withContext(NonCancellable).

deeper.body:
A `CancellationException` doesn't always mean "I was cancelled". If you `await()` a `Deferred` that someone else cancelled, `await` throws `CancellationException` in your coroutine, even though your coroutine is fine. The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 KDoc calls this out as a legacy behavior that can't be changed compatibly: your coroutine then ends as "cancelled", so its parent isn't told and the work silently stops. If you catch it, check `currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()` in the `catch`. It throws only if *your* coroutine was cancelled, so after it you know the exception came from the thing you awaited, and you can turn it into a real error.

The library also gives a **prompt cancellation guarantee**. If a coroutine is cancelled while suspended, it resumes with `CancellationException` even when the value it was waiting for had already arrived. `withContext` checks for cancellation both on entry and when its block returns. So `val conn = withContext(io) { pool.borrow() }` can lose a connection: the block borrowed it, the caller was cancelled in the meantime, and the result is thrown away. Borrow and release inside the same block, or use the `onCancellation` callback of `CancellableContinuation.resume` when you write the bridge yourself (lesson 1 of this track).

Timeouts have one more subtle rule. The KDoc says cancellation on timeout "may happen at any time, even after the block finishes executing but before the caller gets resumed". So never write `withTimeout { resource = open() }` and expect `resource` to be either unset or yours. Open the resource outside the timeout, or close it in the block's own `finally`.

Finally, `runBlocking` bridges in the other direction. If the thread blocked in `runBlocking` is interrupted, the coroutine is cancelled and `runBlocking` throws `InterruptedException`. That is how a coroutine-based Kafka handler called from a plain consumer thread can still be stopped by `shutdownNow()`.
